question: Tungsten is considered for fusion first-wall and divertor service, but it has low strength, limited thermal-shock resistance, a high ductile-brittle transition temperature, and develops dislocation loops and He bubbles under energetic-particle exposure that increase hardening and brittleness; subsequent annealing does not fully remove the damage. Earlier efforts based on cold rolling, wire drawing, and severe plastic deformation sought to improve W, yet fracture resistance remains unresolved and nanocrystalline W still suffers severe damage. Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 showed better radiation resistance than nanocrystalline W and negligible hardening, but Cr-V-rich precipitates appeared at 8 dpa. W29Ta42Cr5V16Hf8 showed neither dislocation loops nor precipitates at 10 dpa, while its greater number of constituents complicates bulk fabrication; the low melting point of Cr also impairs fabrication feasibility in both compositions. For nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exposed to energetic particles near 8 dpa, what single intervention could suppress precipitate formation while preserving low hardening, radiation resistance, and practical bulk manufacturability? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predict measurable outcomes against the unmodified baseline, define dose and specimen-temperature limits, identify supporting observations from the prior work summarized above, and specify a controlled exposure and post-exposure characterization experiment whose results would falsify the hypothesis.
